items.text: Chatbot, workflow, agent: who decides the next step
Four parts: model, instructions, tools, state
The loop: decide, act, observe, repeat, with a limit
Tool errors are observations; tools use allow-lists
Every ending has one clear reason

scenes.question: The resume analyzer from Module 3 always runs extract, compare, advise. What is it?
scenes.explain: Its steps are fixed and chosen by code, so it's a workflow. In an agent, the model chooses the steps.

scenes.question: What does `stop_reason == "tool_use"` mean?
options: The model wants your program to run a tool
The API ran the tool for you
scenes.explain: The model stopped to request a tool. Your program runs it and sends back a tool_result.

scenes.question: Where do tool results go in the message list?
options: In a user message, as tool_result blocks with matching ids
scenes.explain: Results go in the next user message, one tool_result per request, matched by tool_use_id.

scenes.question: Why should the loop be `for turn in range(max_steps)` instead of `while True`?
options: It guarantees the agent stops, even if the model never finishes
The API limits loops to 6 turns
while True doesn't work in Python
scenes.explain: A model can get stuck calling tools. A step limit always ends the loop, and limits cost.

scenes.question: Why does the calculator use an AST allow-list instead of eval()?
options: eval runs any Python code, so tool input could do anything
scenes.explain: Tool input is untrusted. An allow-list permits only arithmetic and refuses everything else.

captions.text: Welcome back.
The agent works.
Now we make it easy to watch, run a bigger demo, break it on purpose, and test it.
Then we'll wrap up the module with a quiz and your extension challenge.
A trace prints what the agent does while it works.
For each step: an act line with the tool and its input, and an observe line with the
result.
An equals sign means success, an exclamation mark means an error.
Ask builds the agent and runs it, passing show step as the on step callback, so each
step prints as soon as it happens.
The summary line, with turns, tool calls, and cost, goes to standard error, so it
never mixes with the answer.
And if the agent stopped for any reason other than answering, that reason becomes
one clear error message, with exit code one.
Now a bigger question, with three pieces of work: a price with a tip, a split three
ways, and a marathon distance in miles.
Read the trace from the top.
Act: calculate eighteen times one point one five.
Observe: twenty point seven.
Act: divide by three.
Observe: six point nine.
Act: convert forty-two point one nine five kilometres to miles.
Observe: twenty-six point two miles.
Four turns, three tool calls.
A real model would also write a friendly final sentence.
Offline, the placeholder lists the results.
Pause and look at that trace again.
Which tool call would change if the tip were twenty percent instead of fifteen?
And which other results would change after it?
The first call changes: eighteen times one point two.
And so does the split, because it uses that result.
The marathon conversion doesn't change at all.
Reading a trace like this is how you debug agents.
Now let's break things on purpose.
Kilograms to kilometres makes no sense.
The convert tool refuses with a clear reason, cannot convert mass to length, and the
agent still finishes.
A real model would explain the problem to the user.
A refusal ends the loop with one clear line.
And a rejected API key does too.
No tracebacks anywhere.
The tests run the real loop and the real tools against the fake.
This first one checks the full run: which tools were used, their outputs, and the
number of turns.
This one checks what was sent: the tools, the system prompt, and the history growing
from one message to three.
This checks the rule from lesson three: each tool result carries the same ID as the
request it answers.
And these test the safety from lesson four: recovering from a tool error, and
stopping at the step limit.
Thirty-four tests, all passing, with no key and no network.
They include seven dangerous or invalid expressions that the calculator must refuse.
And mypy is happy with every type hint.
If the agent stops after too many turns, read the trace.
If it repeats the same call, the tool's error message probably isn't clear enough.
Only raise the step limit if the task really needs more.
If the model answers without using the tools, check that the description and the
instructions say clearly when to use them.
A four hundred error about tool use IDs means a result is missing, or its ID doesn't
match.
Every request needs its result, in the next user message.
And placeholder answers mean you're offline.
That's expected.
Set your API key to use Claude.
Chatbots, workflows, and agents differ in who decides the next step.
Every agent has four parts: the model, the instructions, the tools, and the state.
The loop decides, acts, observes, and repeats, always with a limit.
Tool errors are observations, and tools use allow lists.
And every ending has one clear reason.
Module quiz, question one.
The resume analyzer always runs extract, compare, then advise.
What is it?
A workflow.
Its steps are fixed, and chosen by code.
Question two.
What does a stop reason of tool use mean?
The model wants your program to run a tool.
Your program runs it, and sends back the result.
Question three.
Where do tool results go?
In the next user message, as tool result blocks, each with the matching ID.
Question four.
Why give the loop a limit, instead of while true?
It guarantees the agent stops, even if the model never finishes, and it limits the
cost.
And question five.
Why does the calculator use an allow list, instead of eval?
Because eval runs any Python code at all.
Tool input is untrusted, so we allow only arithmetic, and refuse everything else.
Your extension challenge.
Pick one or more, and write a test for each, using the fake API.
Add a percent of tool, with its own definition and errors.
Add a JSON option that prints the steps and the answer as JSON.
Stop early if the model repeats exactly the same tool call twice in a row.
Or, with an API key, run five word problems on a real model, and compare the traces.
